definition: The small jolt of discovering that a smooth, plausible machine answer is false; the moment trust recalibrates.
etymology: From truth (Old English trēowth, ‘faithfulness’) and flinch (Old French flenchir, ‘to bend’). Both halves are older than they look: truth meant fidelity before it meant fact, and flinch was a bending before it was a recoil — the give in a thing that had been holding. So the compound says more than the shock of an error. It says that something you were faithful to has bent, and bent things do not come back to quite where they were.
in_use: I had my first truthflinch when it invented a Dickens quote. Now I verifidget everything.
the_case: Every name we have for the error — hallucination, confabulation, the fabricated citation — describes what the machine did, and none describes what happened to you. Truthflinch names the second thing: the half-second before the correction and before the shrug, when a piece of trust you had not noticed you were carrying turns out to have a hole in it. It is a noun because it is an event — you can count them, date them, remember the first, and most people can. It is also the thing that actually teaches: nobody ever learned from the small print under the box, in the way nobody learns from a sign saying the floor may be wet. What teaches is the slip. Trust does not collapse, it recalibrates — to a setting with the checking built in.
seo_title: truthflinch — the jolt when a confident AI answer turns out false
seo_description: It gave you the year, the page and the translator’s name; a week later the page was about something else. Truthflinch names the half-second in which trust recalibrates.
